ogTitle: Phuket Beach Itinerary: Kata, Karon, Big Buddha & Promthep
ogDesc: A smooth-flowing plan down Phuket's south coast, ending with sunset at Promthep Cape
intro: The south coast of Phuket packs the good stuff close together, just a few minutes apart by car. Kata and Karon have white sand and clear water, the Three Bays viewpoint lines up three beaches in a single frame, the Big Buddha on Nakkerd Hill reopened to visitors on 3 March 2026, and you close out the day with sunset at Promthep Cape. We've mapped this out hour by hour so each stop flows into the next, and it works as either a 2-day or a 3-day trip.

blocks.html: The Kata–Karon–Rawai beach zone sits on the south of the island, about 18–20 km from Phuket Town and roughly a 30–40 minute drive south of Patong. The upside is that the main sights — the beaches, the viewpoint, the Big Buddha, and Promthep Cape — all fall within a 15 km radius. Base yourself around Kata or Karon and you can loop through the whole day without ever crossing the island.

This plan suits anyone who wants an easy trip centred on the sea and the views, with no boat rides out to the islands. Pack a swimsuit, sunscreen, and a shawl or sarong (for the Big Buddha). A rental car or motorbike is the easiest way around, since Phuket taxis and ride services run pricey and can be hard to flag down at certain times.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Kata & Karon beaches + the Three Bays viewpoint

blocks.html: Spend the first day right on the water. Swim at Kata in the morning, move over to Karon in the afternoon, then catch the Three Bays viewpoint in the soft late-afternoon light.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Working the coast: Kata to Karon

items.activity: Start the morning at Kata Beach
items.note: Fine white sand, clear water, and gentle waves in the morning — good for swimming and beginner surfing. There are stalls renting deckchairs and umbrellas along the sand.

items.activity: Coffee with a sea view at The Commune Terrace & Bar on the Kata hillside
items.note: A café-bar up on the slope with a full view over Kata Bay, serving drinks and pizza. Coffee starts around ฿90–140, and there's a chilled DJ set in the evenings.

items.activity: Southern Thai lunch at Suan Jai Khiao
items.note: A café-restaurant on the Kata hillside doing khanom jeen nam ya and bold southern Thai dishes, with a view down over Kata Beach and the Andaman Sea.
The longest beach in the zone, with white sand that squeaks underfoot and fewer crowds than Kata — good for sunbathing and an afternoon swim.

items.activity: Head up to the Three Bays viewpoint (Karon Viewpoint)
items.note: You see three beaches in graded shades — Kata Noi, Kata, and Karon — curving like a crescent moon. Free, open 24 hours, best in the late-afternoon light, with parking along the road.

items.activity: Seafood dinner in Rawai or Karon
items.note: Rawai has seafood spots where you pick your own catch and have it cooked fresh — prawns and crab are priced by weight, so always check the price before you order.

blocks.title: A note on the surf
blocks.html: During the monsoon (roughly May–October), the waves at Kata and Karon pick up and rip currents form. Always check the warning flags before you go in — a red flag means don't swim. In high season (November–April) the sea is calmer and easier to swim in.

blocks.html: Day two covers the south-coast landmarks. Climb Nakkerd Hill to the Big Buddha in the morning before the sun gets harsh, stop by a temple and a beach in the afternoon, then close the day at Promthep Cape for sunset — widely held to be the best spot on the island to watch the sun drop below the horizon.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Big Buddha + closing the day at Promthep Cape

items.activity: Up to the Big Buddha (Wat Kittisangkharam)
items.note: A 45-metre white-marble statue on top of Nakkerd Hill, overlooking Chalong Bay and the south coast. It reopened to visitors on 3 March 2026 after closing for repairs following a landslide. Free entry (donations accepted).

items.activity: Dress modestly before going up to the statue
items.note: You need to cover your shoulders and knees — no sleeveless tops or short trousers/skirts. There are free sarongs to borrow at the entrance if you forget.

items.activity: On the way down, stop at Wat Chalong (Wat Chaiyathararam)
items.note: The most revered temple among Phuket locals, with a beautiful ordination hall and pagoda. It's right on the route back down from the Big Buddha toward the south. Free entry.
Rawai has both seafood restaurants and local eateries — grab a seat by the water and catch the breeze before the afternoon.

items.activity: Relax at Nai Harn or Rawai Beach
items.note: Nai Harn is quiet with clear water and sits just before Promthep Cape — good for a swim or lazing about while you wait for the late-afternoon light.

items.activity: Arrive at Promthep Cape and stake out a sunset spot
items.note: Aim to get there 1–2 hours before sunset, as traffic builds and the car park fills fast. There's the Kanchanaphisek Lighthouse to climb for a panoramic view.

items.activity: Watch the sunset from the tip of the cape
items.note: A sunset spot reckoned to be among the finest in Thailand. From November to April the skies are clear and the view is sharp. Get your photos, then head down gradually to dodge the traffic.

blocks.title: On the Big Buddha after its reopening
blocks.html: The Big Buddha reopened in March 2026 after a long closure following a 2024 landslide. Access can still be uncertain at times and construction work is ongoing. It's worth checking the status again on the day you plan to go, and keeping a backup plan in case of an unscheduled closure.

blocks.text: If you have 3 days, what to add

blocks.html: If you've covered the south coast over two days and still have time, the third day can drift a little further north or head out on a boat to the islands — depending on whether you want to relax or go all in.

blocks.label: Day 3
blocks.title: Take it easy or go all in

items.activity: Go all in: a day-trip boat tour to Phi Phi or Phang Nga Bay
items.note: Boats leave Rawai Pier or Chalong Bay in the morning and return in the evening. Book ahead for a better rate.

items.activity: Take it easy: walk Phuket Old Town and its Sino-Portuguese buildings
items.note: Thalang and Dibuk roads are colourful and full of cafés and local food. It's about a 30–40 minute drive from Kata into town.

items.activity: Tick off a beach you haven't reached yet, like Nai Harn or Yanui
items.note: Small, quiet beaches in the south with few people and clear water — a calm way to wrap up the trip.

items.activity: A farewell meal of Phuket's local dishes
items.note: Try Hokkien mee, oh tao (oyster omelette), or morning dim sum — the local specialities Phuket is genuinely known for.

items: Big Buddha entry — free (there's a donation box toward the construction fund)
Three Bays viewpoint / Promthep Cape — both free, no entrance fee
Daily car rental — cars from around ฿900–1,500/day; motorbikes around ฿250–350/day (you should carry an international driving permit and wear a helmet)
Deckchair + beach umbrella — around ฿100–150 per set per day, negotiable
Meals — local eateries around ฿80–150 a plate; seafood priced by weight depending on the catch, so ask the price before you order

faq.q: Is the Big Buddha in Phuket open to visitors in 2026?
faq.a: Yes. The Big Buddha (Wat Kittisangkharam) reopened to visitors on 3 March 2026, after closing for repairs following a 2024 landslide. Entry is free, and it's open roughly from 8am into the evening — but access can still be uncertain at times, so check the status before you go.

faq.q: What time should I arrive at Promthep Cape for sunset?
faq.a: Aim to arrive 1–2 hours before sunset, so from around 16:30 onward, because traffic builds and the car park fills up fast near sundown. November through April has the clearest skies, with a sharp view of the sun dropping below the sea.

faq.q: What should I wear to visit the Big Buddha in Phuket?
faq.a: You need to dress modestly, covering your shoulders and knees — no sleeveless tops or short trousers or skirts. If you forget, there are free sarongs to borrow at the entrance.

faq.q: How many days do I need for Kata–Karon and Promthep Cape?
faq.a: Two days is about right. Spend the first on Kata and Karon beaches plus the Three Bays viewpoint, and the second on the Big Buddha and Promthep Cape. If you have a third day, add an island boat tour or a walk around Phuket Old Town.

faq.q: Which area should I stay in for the south-coast beaches?
faq.a: Staying around Kata or Karon is the most convenient, since it sits in the middle of the beaches, the viewpoint, the Big Buddha, and Promthep Cape. You can drive to every stop within a 15 km radius without crossing the island.
